newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Israeli cabinet approves settlement incentives.
newsitem.headline: Israeli cabinet approves settlement incentives.

text.p: The Israeli government on Friday agreed to grant financial benefits to Jewish settlers in the West Bank, a move that could entice more Israelis to settle in the occupied area.

The decision, two days after Palestinian gunmen killed two settlers, was a strong sign of defiance by right-wing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to world opposition to his plans to tighten Israel's hold on captured Arab land.

"This decision is a direct call for violence and a declaration of war on the Palestinian people and its National Authority. It threatens to undermine what remains of the peace process," the Palestinian Information Ministry said.

At its weekly meeting, the cabinet decided to reinstate benefits for West Bank settlers, such as lower taxes, that are already given to residents of so-called development towns inside Israel, to Israelis in Gaza and to those in the occupied Golan Heights.

"The rest of the communities in Judea and Samaria (the West Bank) will enjoy the benefits of "A"-level national priority area status," a cabinet communique said. The West Bank incentives were cancelled after the Labour party came to power in 1992.

Army radio said Finance Minister Dan Meridor, who on Monday had pushed through the cabinet a plan to cut state spending in 1997 by 6.1 billion shekels ($1.9 billion), demanded to know at Friday's session how it would pay for the benefits.
He received no immediate answer. The cabinet statement said the benefits would be implementated after a ministrial committee headed by Netanyahu works out the details.
More than 130,000 Jewish settlers live among nearly two million Arabs in the West Bank and Gaza Strip.
"In practical terms, it does not add an additional house," government spokesman Moshe Fogel said about the incentive plan.
But a settlement drive under previous right-wing Likud leadership in the 1980s was fuelled in part by housing grants for Israelis who could not afford a red-roofed villa near Israel's major towns.
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat said in Gaza on Thursday the addition of even one house to a Jewish settlement would be a violation of his peace deals with Israel.

"Peace and security will not be achieved by making this area (the West Bank) a 'national priority region'. It is simply a joke," said former Housing Minister Binyamin Ben-Eliezer, a member of the previous Labour-led government.
"Talking about building new settlements and thousands of housing units is tantamount to ending the Oslo (peace) process," he told the radio.

Since taking office in June, the Netanyahu government has given the go-ahead for the construction of thousands of homes in existing settlements but has yet to meet the demands of settler leaders to establish new outposts.
Settler leaders welcomed Friday's decision but said it did not go far enough.
"It is a Zionist answer but not enough of a Zionist answer," settler spokesman Aharon Domb said, demanding the government approve new settlements.

In another challenge to Netanyahu, the armed wing of the militant Moslem group Hamas, hit hard by PLO and Israeli crackdowns, said on Friday it would mark the first anniversary of the killing of its master bombmaker by renewing attacks against Israel.

"Our response to the martyrdom of the giant engineer on his first anniversary will be strong, very painful and a major challenge to the state of the Zionist entity with all its army, forces, security and war supplies," it said in a statement faxed to an international news agency.
Bombmaker Yahya Ayyash was killed last January 5 in Gaza when his booby-trapped cellular telephone exploded. The assassination is widely believed to have been carried out by Israel.
($1 = 3.28 shekels)
